newsitem.title: GERMANY: G7 seen getting higher dlr whether it wants or not.
newsitem.headline: G7 seen getting higher dlr whether it wants or not.

text.p: The Group of Seven (G7) industrial nations, having witnessed months of relentless dollar strength following years of weakness, pronounced on Satruday that the currency market had finally straightened itself out.

But analysts were left with the impression it might tolerate even more dollar appreciation. They said as long as G7 leaders do not explicitly talk the dollar back down, the economic fundamentals will favour a higher dollar.
"They're not saying the dollar is over-extended and has to go down," said Graham McDevitt, senior analyst at Paribas Capital Markets in London.
McDevitt said "obviously behind the closet," G7 members would like to see at least a slower dollar. "But they're not talking it down."
Finance ministers and central bank governors form G7, which includes the United States, Germany, Japan, Britain, France, Italy and Canada, held a one-day meeting here on Saturday.
They issued a brief statement afterwards saying the major currency misalignments they had noted in April 1995 had been corrected.

Markets went into this meeting thinking the G7 might be setting the dollar up for a fall. Since the start of 1997, it has already climbed some 12 pfennigs and seven yen to trade at 1.6600 marks and 122.90 yen in late Europe on Friday.

When those levels are compared to levels around the time of the April 1995 G7 communique, the dollar's performance is even more spectacular. It has climbed more than 50 percent against the yen from a post-World War Two low of 79.70 and nearly 25 percent against the mark from just over 1.34 marks.
As a result, the market expected that by now, Japanese officials, faced with skittish financial markets at home, might prefer a sturdier yen as further weakness could have a destabilising effect.
"The fear was that there may be a statement that the dollar has gone far enough," said Adrian Owens, international economist at Bank Julius Baer in London.
But in light of the G7's lack of a dynamic statement calling for a dollar retreat, Owens said more gains against the yen and mark were likely.
He said that even though some G7 countries would not mind a stronger dollar, the rich nations' club had to be careful.

"They have to be careful because we all know that foreign exchange markets tend to overshoot," Owens said. Any G7 wording suggesting it would like a higher dollar could send the dollar skyrocketing, he said.

G7 ministers said they did not see the need for any agreement on intervention in the foreign exchange markets, a tactic which has produced mixed results over the years. However, they noted the G7 does stand ready to take action if need be.
German central bank governor Hans Tietmeyer said after the meeting that the G7 had not discussed using intervention.
Britain's finance minister Kenneth Clarke said the G7 did not deem it necessary.
"We reached no agreement of that kind today," Clarke said. "We didn't think it was necessary."

McDevitt of Paribas said the G7 probably would like to see the dollar consolidate its gains. "They think that in the big picture, it's reached a level where they're happy with it, and they'd like the volatility to die away."
He said the dollar's spending some time in ranges of about 120.00 to 125.00 yen and 1.60 to 1.70 marks would be ideal to the G7.

But McDevitt noted good reasons for a higher dollar. Japan, for instance, has already cut and held its official discount rate at a record low 0.5 percent since September 1995 and has gone to great lengths to add fiscal stimulus. "They really had no option but to let the yen go," he said.
U.S. and European economic trends were also prodding the dollar higher, analysts said.
"The fundamentals still favour the dollar," said Esther Baroudy, economist at G.E. Investments (U.S.) in London.
Germany's sluggish economy and worries about Europe's plans for a single currency were set against a healthy U.S. economy, she said. "That contrast will continue to play."
